title: Prepositions after nouns
subtitle: satisfaction with / pride in / respect for
summary: Learn which preposition follows a noun, and when a noun is followed by of + -ing and when by a to-infinitive.

lesson.heading: The same preposition as the adjective or verb
lesson.text: Many nouns take the same preposition as the adjective or verb they are related to, so if you know one you know the other.

examples.text: Are you **satisfied with** the way that the business is being run?
The shareholders have expressed **satisfaction with** the way the business is being run.

lesson.heading: A few nouns change the preposition
lesson.text: A few nouns take a different preposition from their related adjective, so they have to be learnt as pairs.

examples.text: They became **fond of** each other at school.
Their **fondness for** each other grew and many years later they married.

lesson.note: Also: proud of / pride in, ashamed of / shame about / at.

lesson.heading: Nouns that need a preposition when the verb does not
lesson.text: Some verbs take a direct object, but the related noun needs a preposition. Many other nouns are followed by an *of* phrase that shows possession or classifies the noun.

examples.text: He **described** the conductor as moving his arms like a windmill.
His **description of** the conductor was very funny.

lesson.note: Also: admiration for, ban on, discussion about / on, improvement in, influence on, interview with, lack of, respect for.

lesson.heading: of + -ing or a to-infinitive?

left.label: of + -ing (not usually a to-infinitive)
left.text: Nouns about likelihood, danger and evidence.
examples: He's got into the **habit of biting** his nails when he's nervous.
Also: cost, effect, fear, likelihood, possibility, probability, problem, prospect, risk, sign.

right.label: to-infinitive (not usually of + -ing)
right.text: Nouns about willingness, ability and choice.
examples: His unhappy childhood explains his **reluctance to talk** about his parents.
Also: ability, attempt, concern, decision, desire, determination, failure, inability, permission, proposal, reason, refusal, (un)willingness.

lesson.note: Many of these nouns work with other prepositions + -ing too: attempt at -ing, reason for -ing.

lesson.heading: Nouns that allow both
lesson.text: After some nouns, usually with *the*, either form is possible with much the same meaning.

examples.text: Do staff have the **opportunity of taking** unpaid leave?
The **aim of providing** clean drinking water has been achieved.

lesson.heading: chance, sense and way - the meaning decides
lesson.text: These nouns have more than one meaning, and each meaning takes its own form.

examples.text: What's the **chance of getting** five heads when you toss a coin five times?
Will you get the **chance to visit** Miki in Japan?
He didn't have the **sense to move** away from the puddle of water as the bus went past.
She had a **sense of belonging** within a few days of moving to her new school.
I've got a new **way to cook** rice. (= method; or way of cooking) / She has a really funny **way of speaking**.

lesson.heading: intention
lesson.text: **of + -ing** usually follows *no / every / the sole / the slightest / (not) any / with the* + intention. In most other cases either form is possible.

examples.text: I have **no intention of lending** Dan any more money.
He announced his **intention to stand** in the election.

lesson.text: When a noun could take either form, ask which meaning you want: a likelihood or feeling takes of + -ing, an opportunity or a piece of judgement takes a to-infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Match each noun with the phrase that follows it.

pairs.right: about the relative merits of CDs and records

exercises.prompt: Yasemin is still in hospital, but over the last couple of days there has been an ___ her condition.
exercises.explanation: The noun improvement takes in, although the verb improve takes no preposition.

exercises.prompt: Rashid takes great ___ his cooking, and is always eager to talk about his recipes.
exercises.explanation: proud of, but pride in - one of the pairs that change preposition.

exercises.prompt: Benny Carter had a significant ___ the development of British jazz.
exercises.explanation: The verb influence takes a direct object, but the noun needs on.

exercises.prompt: Is the noun followed by of + -ing or by a to-infinitive?
The snow has been falling now for two days and shows no ___.
The government has defended its ___ coal mining in the national park.
The exercise tests children's ___ a random sequence of numbers.
What's the ___ five heads when you toss a coin five times?
exercises.explanation: Here chance means likelihood, so it takes of + -ing.

exercises.statement: I have no intention to lend Dan any more money.
exercises.explanation: I have no intention of lending Dan any more money. After no intention we use of + -ing.

exercises.prompt: It's hard to work with Nik because of his ___ that he ever makes mistakes.
Will you get the ___ Miki in Japan?
exercises.explanation: Here chance means opportunity, so it takes a to-infinitive.
